name: Terminate TLS at the Ingress
objective: CKS › Cluster Setup. Drill EVERY corner of terminating TLS at the Ingress harder than the exam: build a kubernetes.io/tls Secret from a self-signed cert, wire a spec.tls block, pin the backend rule, bind an ingressClassName, keep tls hosts aligned with rule hosts, rotate the cert in place under the same name, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix on a broken Ingress. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Create a kubernetes.io/tls Secret
questions.teach:
An Ingress terminates HTTPS using a Secret of type **`kubernetes.io/tls`** holding exactly two keys: **`tls.crt`** and **`tls.key`**. The quick path is `kubectl create secret tls <name> --cert=<file> --key=<file>`, which sets the type and both keys in one shot.

**Gotcha:** the API validates the pair on create — a key that doesn't match the cert is rejected.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `ingress-learn`, generate a self-signed cert + key on the host for CN `demo.example.com`, then create a TLS Secret named `web-tls` from them.

Target: Secret `web-tls` is type `kubernetes.io/tls` and has both `tls.crt` and `tls.key`, and the cert's subject CN is `demo.example.com`.
questions.hint: `openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt -days 365 -subj "/CN=demo.example.com"`, then `kubectl -n ingress-learn create secret tls web-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key`.
questions.solution:
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt -days 365 -subj "/CN=demo.example.com"
kubectl -n ingress-learn create secret tls web-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key
kubectl -n ingress-learn get secret web-tls -o jsonpath='{.type}'   # kubernetes.io/tls

verification.description: Secret web-tls: type kubernetes.io/tls, has tls.crt+tls.key, cert CN demo.example.com

questions.eli5:
When a website says "https," there's a padlock made of two matching pieces: a **certificate** (the public ID card everyone can see, proving "I really am demo.example.com") and a **private key** (the secret only the server knows, which proves it owns that ID). The two are a matched pair — like a lock and the one key that opens it.

In this step you first *manufacture* that pair with `openssl` (self-signed, meaning you're your own authority — fine for practice). Then you hand both pieces to Kubernetes by packing them into a special kind of Secret. `kubectl create secret tls web-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key` does three things at once: it names the Secret `web-tls`, stamps it with the type `kubernetes.io/tls`, and stores the cert under the key `tls.crt` and the private key under `tls.key`.

That `kubernetes.io/tls` type is special: Ingress controllers know to look for exactly those two keys, `tls.crt` and `tls.key`, when they serve HTTPS.

**Watch out for:**

- A TLS Secret must hold **exactly two keys**: `tls.crt` and `tls.key` — those literal names.
- The cert and key must be a **matching pair**. Kubernetes validates this on create and **rejects** a mismatched pair outright.
- The **CN** (Common Name) you pass to openssl (`/CN=demo.example.com`) must be the hostname you'll serve, or browsers warn about a name mismatch later.
- `-nodes` in openssl means "no DES" = don't password-protect the key; the controller needs an unencrypted key.
- The Secret lives in a namespace; create it in `ingress-learn`, the same place the Ingress will live.
questions.deepDive:
## Creating a `kubernetes.io/tls` Secret — full rundown

### Mental model
TLS termination needs a **certificate** (public, identifies the server) and a **private key** (secret, proves ownership). Kubernetes stores this pair in a Secret of the special type **`kubernetes.io/tls`**, which **requires exactly two data keys**: `tls.crt` and `tls.key`. Ingress controllers look for precisely those keys. `kubectl create secret tls` sets the type and both keys in one command and validates that the key matches the cert.

### Generate a self-signed cert + key
```bash
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes \
  -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt \
  -days 365 -subj "/CN=demo.example.com"
```
| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `req -x509` | make a self-signed certificate (not a CSR) |
| `-newkey rsa:2048` | generate a fresh 2048-bit RSA key |
| `-nodes` | "no DES" — do **not** encrypt the key (controllers need it unencrypted) |
| `-keyout` / `-out` | where to write key / cert |
| `-days 365` | validity window |
| `-subj "/CN=demo.example.com"` | set the subject Common Name |

Add Subject Alternative Names (modern clients rely on SAN, not CN):
```bash
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt -days 365 \
  -subj "/CN=demo.example.com" \
  -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:demo.example.com"
```

### Create the Secret
```bash
kubectl -n ingress-learn create secret tls web-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key
```
Equivalent explicit form (what the type looks like underneath):
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: web-tls
  namespace: ingress-learn
type: kubernetes.io/tls
data:
  tls.crt: <base64 of the PEM cert>
  tls.key: <base64 of the PEM key>
```

### Inspect / verify
```bash
kubectl -n ingress-learn get secret web-tls -o jsonpath='{.type}'; echo   # kubernetes.io/tls
kubectl -n ingress-learn get secret web-tls -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' | base64 -d | \
  openssl x509 -noout -subject -enddate
# subject=CN = demo.example.com
# notAfter=...
```
Confirm the key matches the cert (modulus must be identical):
```bash
openssl x509 -noout -modulus -in tls.crt | openssl md5
openssl rsa  -noout -modulus -in tls.key | openssl md5   # same hash -> they match
```

### The data keys — exact names
| Key | Contents |
|---|---|
| `tls.crt` | PEM certificate (optionally a chain: leaf first, then intermediates) |
| `tls.key` | PEM private key, **unencrypted** |

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Exactly `tls.crt` and `tls.key`** — a Secret of this type is invalid without both; other keys are not accepted for TLS use.
- **Mismatched cert/key is rejected at create time** — the API validates the pair, so a wrong key fails immediately.
- **Encrypted (password-protected) keys don't work** — omit the passphrase (`-nodes`), or the controller can't load it.
- **CN alone isn't enough for real clients** — they validate the **SAN**. Add `subjectAltName` or you'll get name-mismatch errors even with TLS working.
- **Namespace matters** — the Secret must live in the same namespace as the Ingress that references it (next steps). A cross-namespace reference is ignored.
- Generic (`kubectl create secret generic`) secrets won't do — the Ingress expects type `kubernetes.io/tls` semantics.
- For a chain, put the **leaf cert first** in `tls.crt`, then intermediates.

### Quick reference
```bash
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt \
  -days 365 -subj "/CN=demo.example.com" -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:demo.example.com"
kubectl -n ingress-learn create secret tls web-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key
kubectl -n ingress-learn get secret web-tls -o jsonpath='{.type}'; echo   # kubernetes.io/tls
```

questions.title: Add a tls block to an Ingress
questions.teach:
An Ingress enables HTTPS via **`spec.tls`** — a list where each entry names a **`secretName`** (the `kubernetes.io/tls` Secret) and the **`hosts`** it covers. For a listed host the controller presents that Secret's cert and terminates TLS at the edge.

**Gotcha:** the `secretName` Secret must live in the **same namespace** as the Ingress — a cross-namespace reference is silently ignored.
questions.prompt:
A Deployment `web` and Service `web` (port 80) already run in `ingress-learn`. Create an Ingress named `web` with a `spec.tls` entry referencing Secret `web-tls` for host `demo.example.com` (include a rule routing that host to Service `web`:80).

Target: Ingress `web` has a `spec.tls` entry whose `secretName` is `web-tls` and whose `hosts` includes `demo.example.com`.
questions.hint: Add `spec.tls: [{hosts: [demo.example.com], secretName: web-tls}]` to the Ingress. Author the full Ingress (rules + tls) in one manifest and `kubectl apply -f -`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: ingress-learn
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - demo.example.com
    secretName: web-tls
  rules:
  - host: demo.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web
            port:
              number: 80
EOF

verification.description: Ingress web spec.tls references secretName web-tls for host demo.example.com

questions.eli5:
You've got the padlock (the Secret). Now you tell the front door of your cluster — the **Ingress** — to actually use it. An Ingress is like a receptionist at the building entrance who reads the address on each visitor ("which website do you want?") and sends them to the right office inside.

To make that receptionist speak HTTPS, you add a `spec.tls` block. It's basically a note that says: *"For visitors asking for `demo.example.com`, show them the padlock stored in the Secret named `web-tls`."* Two pieces per entry: `hosts` (which hostnames this cert covers) and `secretName` (where the cert lives). The receptionist then does the HTTPS handshake at the door and passes plain traffic onward — that's "terminating TLS at the edge."

**Watch out for:**

- The `secretName` Secret must be in the **same namespace** as the Ingress. Point it across namespaces and it's **silently ignored** — no error, just no cert.
- `spec.tls` enables HTTPS, but you still need a matching **rule** (next step) to actually route the host somewhere — list both in one manifest.
- The names must line up: the host in `tls.hosts` should match the host in your routing `rules`, or that host won't get the cert.
- A typo'd `secretName` (pointing at a Secret that doesn't exist) means no cert loads and the controller falls back to plain HTTP or a default cert.
- Each `tls` entry can list several hosts; group hosts that a single cert covers.
questions.deepDive:
## Adding a `spec.tls` block to an Ingress — full rundown

### Mental model
An Ingress terminates HTTPS at the cluster edge: the controller presents a certificate, completes the TLS handshake with the client, then forwards (usually plain HTTP) to the backend Service. `spec.tls` is the list that wires **which hosts** get **which certificate Secret**. Each entry is `{ hosts: [...], secretName: <tls-secret> }`.

### The TLS block
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: ingress-learn
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - demo.example.com         # hostnames this cert covers
    secretName: web-tls        # kubernetes.io/tls Secret, SAME namespace
  rules:
  - host: demo.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web
            port:
              number: 80
```

### How TLS entries map to certs
| `spec.tls` entry | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `hosts: [a.example.com]`, `secretName: a-tls` | controller serves `a-tls`'s cert via SNI for `a.example.com` |
| multiple hosts in one entry | one cert (with those SANs) covers all of them |
| multiple entries | controller selects by SNI hostname |
| `tls: [{ secretName: x }]` with **no hosts** | cert used as the **default**/catch-all for the controller |

### Termination vs passthrough
- **Edge termination** (this, the default): controller decrypts; backend sees HTTP. Needs the `kubernetes.io/tls` Secret.
- **SSL passthrough** (nginx annotation `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-passthrough: "true"`): TLS is **not** terminated at the edge — bytes pass to the backend, which does its own TLS. Then `spec.tls`/`secretName` isn't used for that host.

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.tls[*].secretName}{"\n"}{.spec.tls[*].hosts[*]}{"\n"}'
# web-tls
# demo.example.com

# live check once the controller has an address
curl -k --resolve demo.example.com:443:<INGRESS_IP> https://demo.example.com/
openssl s_client -connect <INGRESS_IP>:443 -servername demo.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Same-namespace rule:** `secretName` resolves only within the Ingress's namespace. A Secret in another namespace is **silently ignored** — no cert, no error.
- **TLS ≠ routing:** `spec.tls` enables HTTPS for a host but you still need a `rules` entry to send that host to a backend. List both.
- **Host alignment:** a host in `tls.hosts` with no matching `rules.host` (or vice versa) leaves gaps — the cert or the route won't apply where you expect (next step hardens this).
- **Nonexistent `secretName`:** the controller can't load a cert and falls back to its default/fake cert or plain HTTP; browsers show the wrong/invalid cert.
- **SNI required:** clients must send SNI (hostname) so the controller picks the right cert; `curl --resolve`/`openssl -servername` set it in tests.
- **Correct apiVersion:** `networking.k8s.io/v1` with the `backend.service.name`/`port.number` shape — the old `extensions/v1beta1` `serviceName`/`servicePort` is gone.

### Quick reference
```yaml
spec:
  tls:
  - hosts: [demo.example.com]
    secretName: web-tls        # same namespace as the Ingress
```
```bash
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web -o jsonpath='{.spec.tls[*].secretName}'; echo  # web-tls
```

questions.title: Route the host to the backend Service
questions.teach:
An Ingress **rule** maps a **`host`** to HTTP paths, each with a **`backend.service`** (name + port) and a `pathType` (usually `Prefix`). The rule for `demo.example.com` must point at Service `web` on port `80`.

**Gotcha:** the backend port is the **Service** port (`service.port.number`), not the container's `targetPort` — mixing them routes to nothing.
questions.prompt:
Ensure Ingress `web` routes host `demo.example.com` to Service `web` on port `80` with `pathType: Prefix` at path `/`.

Target: a rule with `host: demo.example.com` has a path with `pathType: Prefix`, path `/`, and `backend.service.name=web`, port `80`.
questions.hint: Check `kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web -o yaml` for `spec.rules[*].host` and `spec.rules[*].http.paths[*]`. The step-2 manifest already includes this rule; re-apply if missing.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web -o yaml
# rule host demo.example.com, path / (Prefix) -> service web:80 (apply the step-2 manifest if absent)

verification.description: Ingress rule host demo.example.com: path / Prefix routes to service web:80

questions.eli5:
The `tls` block handles the padlock, but it doesn't tell the receptionist *where to send visitors* once they're in. That's what a **rule** does: it's the forwarding instruction. "Anyone asking for `demo.example.com`, take path `/`, and walk them to the `web` office on door number `80`."

A rule has three moving parts: the **host** (which website name), the **path** + **pathType** (which URLs — `/` with `Prefix` means "everything under /"), and the **backend** (which Service and port to hand off to). Here you make sure the rule for `demo.example.com` points at Service `web` on port `80`.

The classic trap is the port number. You give the **Service's** port here (80), not the port inside the container. A Service port and the container's `targetPort` can be different numbers; the Ingress talks to the Service, so it needs the Service's number.

**Watch out for:**

- The backend port is the **Service port** (`service.port.number`), not the container's `targetPort`. Mixing them routes traffic into a black hole.
- `pathType: Prefix` with `path: /` matches everything; the field is required in `networking.k8s.io/v1`.
- The rule's **host** must match the host in your `tls` block so the cert and the route cover the same name.
- The backend Service must actually exist in the same namespace and have that port, or the Ingress has nowhere to send traffic.
- One Ingress can hold many rules (different hosts/paths); here you just need the one for `demo.example.com`.

## Routing a host to a backend Service with an Ingress rule — full rundown

### Mental model
`spec.tls` decides *how* a host is secured; `spec.rules` decides *where* its traffic goes. A rule maps a **host** to a set of **paths**, each path targeting a **backend Service + port**. The port is the **Service** port, not the container's `targetPort`.

### Anatomy of a rule
```yaml
spec:
  rules:
  - host: demo.example.com          # match on SNI/Host header
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix            # required field
        backend:
          service:
            name: web               # Service name (same namespace)
            port:
              number: 80            # SERVICE port, not targetPort
```

### Service port vs targetPort (the classic trap)
```yaml
# Service
spec:
  ports:
  - port: 80           # <-- Ingress references THIS (service.port.number: 80)
    targetPort: 8080   # container's listening port (NOT referenced by the Ingress)
```
The Ingress sends to the **Service**, which then forwards to `targetPort`. Reference `80` in the Ingress; the Service handles the hop to `8080`.

### pathType values
| `pathType` | Matches |
|---|---|
| `Prefix` | path prefix split on `/` — `/` matches everything; `/app` matches `/app`, `/app/x` |
| `Exact` | the exact path string only |
| `ImplementationSpecific` | controller-defined (e.g. nginx regex) |

`pathType` is **mandatory** in `networking.k8s.io/v1`.

### Named vs numbered backend port
```yaml
backend:
  service:
    name: web
    port:
      name: http        # OR number: 80 — use the Service port's name if it has one
```

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web -o yaml | sed -n '/rules:/,$p'

kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web -o jsonpath='
{range .spec.rules[*]}host={.host}{"\n"}
{range .http.paths[*]}  {.path} ({.pathType}) -> {.backend.service.name}:{.backend.service.port.number}{"\n"}{end}{end}'
# host=demo.example.com
#   / (Prefix) -> web:80

# the Service and its endpoints must exist
kubectl -n ingress-learn get svc web -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[*].port}'; echo   # 80
kubectl -n ingress-learn get endpoints web
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Service port, not targetPort.** Referencing the container port routes to nothing.
- **`pathType` is required** — omitting it is a validation error in `networking.k8s.io/v1`.
- **Host must match the TLS host.** A rule host not present in `spec.tls.hosts` gets routed but not TLS-secured (next step fixes this).
- **Backend Service must exist, in-namespace, with that port** and have ready endpoints, or you get 503s.
- **apiVersion/shape:** `networking.k8s.io/v1` uses `backend.service.name` + `backend.service.port.{number|name}`; the legacy `serviceName`/`servicePort` no longer applies.
- A rule with **no `host`** matches all hostnames (catch-all) — be deliberate about that.
- Path matching is controller-sensitive; `Prefix` with `/` is the safe, portable "match everything."

### Quick reference
```yaml
rules:
- host: demo.example.com
  http:
    paths:
    - path: /
      pathType: Prefix
      backend:
        service: { name: web, port: { number: 80 } }   # SERVICE port
```
```bash
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.rules[0].http.paths[0].backend.service.port.number}'; echo   # 80
```

questions.title: Bind the Ingress to an IngressClass
questions.teach:
An Ingress is acted on by a controller only when it names one via **`spec.ingressClassName`** (e.g. `nginx`), or when a default IngressClass exists. Without a class, no controller claims it and TLS is never served.

**Gotcha:** `spec.ingressClassName` is the modern field; the old `kubernetes.io/ingress.class` annotation is deprecated — set the field.
questions.prompt:
Make sure Ingress `web` explicitly selects the `nginx` ingress class via `spec.ingressClassName` (not the deprecated annotation).

Target: Ingress `web` has `spec.ingressClassName` equal to `nginx`.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n ingress-learn patch ingress web --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"ingressClassName":"nginx"}}'`, or set `spec.ingressClassName: nginx` in the manifest.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n ingress-learn patch ingress web --type=merge -p '{"spec":{"ingressClassName":"nginx"}}'
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web -o jsonpath='{.spec.ingressClassName}'   # nginx
questions.eli5:
You can have a perfectly written Ingress and still have *nothing happen*. Why? Because an Ingress object is just a **request form** — it does nothing until an actual **controller** (like nginx) picks it up and acts on it. In a cluster with several controllers, you have to say which one should handle your form. That's `spec.ingressClassName`.

Think of it like dropping a work order into the right team's inbox. Writing `ingressClassName: nginx` is you stamping the form "FOR: the nginx team." Without that stamp (and without a default team configured to grab unstamped forms), the order just sits in limbo — no controller claims it, no load balancer gets configured, and your HTTPS is never actually served.

There's an old way and a new way to do this. The old way was an annotation (`kubernetes.io/ingress.class`). The modern, correct way is the dedicated field `spec.ingressClassName`.

**Watch out for:**

- Use the **field** `spec.ingressClassName: nginx`, not the deprecated `kubernetes.io/ingress.class` annotation.
- With no class set and no **default** IngressClass in the cluster, no controller claims the Ingress — it silently does nothing.
- The class name (`nginx`) must match an **IngressClass** that actually exists in the cluster, or again nothing handles it.
- Setting both the field and the old annotation to conflicting values is asking for confusion — pick the field.
- You can patch it onto an existing Ingress with a merge patch; you don't have to recreate the whole object.
questions.deepDive:
## Binding an Ingress to an IngressClass — full rundown

### Mental model
An Ingress resource is declarative intent; a **controller** realizes it. `spec.ingressClassName` names the **IngressClass** whose controller should handle this Ingress. A cluster can run multiple controllers (nginx, traefik, cloud LB), so each Ingress must say which one — or rely on a cluster default. No matching class and no default → **no controller claims the Ingress**, and nothing (including TLS) is served.

### The field (modern, correct)
```yaml
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
```
Patch it onto an existing Ingress:
```bash
kubectl -n ingress-learn patch ingress web --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"ingressClassName":"nginx"}}'
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web -o jsonpath='{.spec.ingressClassName}'; echo   # nginx
```

### How IngressClass itself looks
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: IngressClass
metadata:
  name: nginx
  annotations:
    ingressclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"   # optional: makes it the default
spec:
  controller: k8s.io/ingress-nginx     # which controller implements this class
```
```bash
kubectl get ingressclass          # list available classes + their controllers
```

### Field vs deprecated annotation
| Form | Status |
|---|---|
| `spec.ingressClassName: nginx` | **current**, use this |
| annotation `kubernetes.io/ingress.class: nginx` | **deprecated**; some controllers still honour it, but don't rely on it |

If both are set and disagree, behaviour is controller-specific — avoid the conflict; set the field only.

### Default IngressClass
If an IngressClass is marked `is-default-class: "true"`, Ingresses that **omit** `ingressClassName` at creation are assigned it. Caveats:
- Only matters **at admission** — existing Ingresses aren't retro-assigned.
- Exactly one class should be default; multiple defaults is a misconfiguration.

### Verify the controller actually adopted it
```bash
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web          # ADDRESS populates once a controller programs it
kubectl -n ingress-learn describe ingress web     # events from the controller
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Set the field, not the annotation.** Tasks that say "not the deprecated annotation" are checking `spec.ingressClassName`.
- **No class + no default = nothing happens.** The Ingress exists but is never programmed; HTTPS is never served. A classic "my Ingress does nothing" cause.
- **Class name must match an existing IngressClass.** A typo'd class name leaves the Ingress unclaimed.
- **Default is admission-time only** — adding a default later won't adopt already-created class-less Ingresses.
- `ingressClassName` is a top-level `spec` field, **not** under `rules` or `tls`.
- A merge `patch` adds the field without rewriting the object — handy when the rest is already correct.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n ingress-learn patch ingress web --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"ingressClassName":"nginx"}}'
kubectl get ingressclass                                   # confirm "nginx" exists
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web -o jsonpath='{.spec.ingressClassName}'; echo   # nginx
```

questions.title: Keep the tls hosts aligned with the rule hosts
questions.teach:
If a host in `spec.rules` is absent from every `spec.tls.hosts`, the controller serves it over plain HTTP with no cert. Harden the Ingress so **every rule host also appears in some `spec.tls.hosts`** list — here `demo.example.com` must be in both.

**Gotcha:** the cert's CN/SAN must also cover the host, or clients still get a name-mismatch warning even with TLS on.
questions.prompt:
Harden Ingress `web`: ensure every host it routes also has TLS — i.e. every `spec.rules` host is covered by some `spec.tls[*].hosts` entry, with no mismatch.

Target: every host under `spec.rules` appears in `spec.tls[*].hosts` (no routed host is plain-HTTP-only).
questions.hint: Compare `kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web -o jsonpath='{.spec.rules[*].host}'` with `{.spec.tls[*].hosts[*]}`. Every rule host must appear in the tls host set; re-apply a corrected manifest if one is only in rules.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web -o jsonpath='{.spec.rules[*].host}{"\n"}{.spec.tls[*].hosts[*]}{"\n"}'
# every rule host must also appear in a tls hosts list; fix the manifest if one is missing

verification.description: every spec.rules host is covered by a spec.tls hosts entry (no plain-HTTP-only host)

questions.eli5:
Here's a sneaky way to leave a hole: you can route a hostname in your `rules` but forget to list it in `spec.tls`. When that happens, the controller happily serves that host — but over **plain HTTP, with no padlock at all**. Traffic that was supposed to be encrypted goes out in the clear, and nobody warned you.

This step is the hardening check: make sure **every host you route also has TLS**. In other words, every hostname that shows up under `spec.rules` must also appear in some `spec.tls.hosts` list. Here that means `demo.example.com` has to be in *both* places. Think of it like a building where you listed the room on the directory (rules) but forgot to install a lock on its door (tls) — you go back and make sure every listed room is also locked.

**Watch out for:**

- A rule host that's **missing from every `spec.tls.hosts`** is served as plain HTTP — a silent downgrade, no error.
- Compare the two lists directly: every `spec.rules[*].host` must appear in `spec.tls[*].hosts`.
- Even with TLS turned on, the **cert's CN/SAN must cover the host** too — otherwise clients still get a name-mismatch warning. TLS "on" and TLS "correct" are two different things.
- A host can appear in `tls.hosts` with no matching rule — harmless, but it's the reverse direction that creates the security hole.
- Re-apply a corrected manifest if a host was only in `rules`; adding it to a `tls` entry closes the gap.
questions.deepDive:
## Keeping `spec.tls` hosts aligned with `spec.rules` hosts — full rundown

### Mental model
`spec.rules` lists every host the Ingress **routes**. `spec.tls` lists every host it **secures**. If a routed host is absent from every `spec.tls[*].hosts`, the controller still serves it — **over plain HTTP, with no certificate**. That's a silent security downgrade. Hardening means: *every rule host is covered by some TLS host*, and the presented cert's CN/SAN actually matches that host.

### The relationship
| Host appears in… | Result |
|---|---|
| `rules` **and** `tls.hosts` | routed **and** TLS-terminated ✅ |
| `rules` only | routed but **plain HTTP** (no cert) ⚠️ the hole to close |
| `tls.hosts` only | cert configured but nothing routed there (harmless, usually a leftover) |
| neither | not handled at all |

### A correctly aligned Ingress
```yaml
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - demo.example.com          # must include EVERY rule host below
    secretName: web-tls
  rules:
  - host: demo.example.com      # <-- present in tls.hosts above
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service: { name: web, port: { number: 80 } }
```

### Diagnose a mismatch
```bash
# dump both sets and eyeball
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web -o jsonpath='
rules:{range .spec.rules[*]} {.host}{end}{"\n"}
tls:  {range .spec.tls[*]}{range .hosts[*]} {.}{end}{end}{"\n"}'
# rules:  demo.example.com
# tls:    demo.example.com          <- every rule host must appear here
```
Any host in the rules line that's missing from the tls line is being served without TLS — add it to a `spec.tls` entry and re-apply.

### Confirm the cert actually matches the host
TLS "on" is not the same as TLS "valid". The cert's CN/SAN must cover the host:
```bash
openssl s_client -connect <INGRESS_IP>:443 -servername demo.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -ext subjectAltName
# subject=CN = demo.example.com
# X509v3 Subject Alternative Name: DNS:demo.example.com
```
A mismatch here still triggers client name-mismatch warnings even though TLS is enabled.

### Related hardening knobs (context)
- **Force HTTPS:** nginx redirects HTTP→HTTPS by default for TLS-enabled hosts; `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"` makes it explicit. `force-ssl-redirect` redirects even without a matching cert.
- **Default/fake cert:** for a host with no matching `tls` entry/secret, the controller may serve its self-signed default cert — looks "encrypted" but is wrong; don't mistake that for success.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Rule host not in any `tls.hosts` → plain HTTP, silently.** No error is raised; you must compare the two lists yourself.
- **TLS enabled ≠ correct cert.** The cert CN/SAN must also cover the host, or clients still see mismatch warnings.
- The dangerous direction is **rules-without-tls**; tls-without-rules is just unused config.
- Hostnames must match **exactly** (and are case-insensitive DNS names); a stray subdomain in rules needs its own TLS coverage (or a wildcard cert + `*.example.com` SAN).
- After fixing, **re-apply** the whole manifest or patch the `tls` entry; editing only `rules` won't close the gap.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n ingress-learn get ingress web -o jsonpath='{.spec.rules[*].host}{"\n"}{.spec.tls[*].hosts[*]}{"\n"}'
# every host on line 1 MUST appear on line 2
```
